Author: @Sam---1-h7f
Content:
When I was a kid, I used to be amazed with circles and why we don't have laws to calculate it's circumference and area like we have for squares and rectangles (which what I only knew back then).

I spent days trying to measure its  circumference and area using paper and some sewing thread.

I finally came up with constant of K = 1.6 and laws that say 

Circumference = K*D, where D is the circle diameter. 

Area = (K/4)*(D*D), yes I didn't know squares or powers back then.

I took it to my math teacher full of excitement with my discovery, only for him to tell me that I'm 2000 years late to discovery ... and introduce me to Pi.

I was 8 back then living in a 3rd world country, and was so impressed with mathematics. Only if I had a better teacher 🤦‍♂️

Author: @basketcase77
Content:
This yet again shows why Tau is superior to Pi for use. Pi is one half of a turn, while Tau is a full turn, or 2 * Pi. So we use 3.14 radians, but a circle is 6.28 radians in circumference. It really works better across a variety of uses. It's more intuitive to count the sections of a circle as portions of a turn, not portions of twice that, which only causes confusing fraction simplification. Also, circular area is the change in radius, so just like acceleration is 1/2 v^2 as it's the change in velocity, or many other calculus formulas based on FTC, 1/2 Tau^2 makes more sense as well.
Check out the Tau manifesto if you'd like to see why it's superior in every aspect of math, physics, and engineering to use Tau instead of Pi.

Author: @SheepdogSmokey
Content:
I had someone once ask why pizza is round, slices are triangular, and the box is square, and the answers are so simple.

The dough rises in a ball, so the easiest shape to make is a flat circle.

Cutting on the diameter (to make all slices equal) creates triangular pieces.

While circular (and other shaped) boxes exist, they take more time and cost more, the square box is quicker and cheaper to make, and for delivery, you have corners for dipping sauce cups.

All three boil down to quickest and easiest, and thus, cheapest, way to make them.

Author: @bowtiexoxo
Content:
Great explanation, but not perfect. Although the shape's area is L*W, calling it a "rectangle" is inaccurate. A rectangle is a plane figure with four straight sides and four right angles. This shape would have infinite sides and include curved lines.
I think a better alternative would be "rectangular shape" because the definition of rectangular is only "like a rectangle" and not necessarily "a rectangle". The shape is very similar to a rectangle and the word "rectangle" does help with some visualization, but it is not a true rectangle.
Definition from Oxford Languages:
adjective: rectangular
1.
denoting or shaped like a rectangle.
"a neat rectangular area"
(of a solid) having a base, section, or side shaped like a rectangle.
"a rectangular prism"
2.
placed or having parts placed at right angles.

Content:
Circumference = pi × diameter i.e pi × d
Diameter = 2 × radius
So, half Circumference = (pi × 2 × radius)/2

Which is 2 × pi × r/2 = pi × r
So, half Circumference, which is same a the length of the formed rectangle is pi × r.

Width has same length as radius, so area of the circle is pi × r × r = pi × r^2

Content:
Each of those piece you have cut is a triangle shape.
So if there are 25 triangle pieces cut out of that pizza. Each triangle with base is 2πr/25, and height r
Area = 25 x Area of each triangle 

Area of each triangle = 1/2 * B * H
                      = 1/2 * 2πr/25 * r
                      = πr²/25
Area = 25 x Area of each triangle
     = 25 x πr²/25 = πr²

Content: I think that pi shouldn’t be expressed as a number but rather as a ratio. Simply put, no matter how big the diameter of a circle is, the ratio of circumference to the diameter is always 22 to 7. So if a circle has a diameter 7, the circumference is exactly 22. That is a simple way to use pi without involving inaccurate decimals. Author: @tanner_titus
Content:
I didn’t watch the entire video to know whether or not it was explained that circumference = pi • diameter OR 2pi(r). That would have been a good thing to mention for anyone using this clip to understand circles that has no background knowledge. Those of us that already know the formulas but are watching this to have a visual aid as to WHY they are what they are, don’t need to be told that, but a younger person might. 

I say this because when explaining area, it is immediately said that the length is Pi(R). Without the explanation that circumference can also be written as 2pi(r) and when that is divided in half you get Pi(r) representing each length side of the rectangle. It may be confusing where the value of the length comes from and the learner may not get as deep of an understanding as they could. 

You can infer all of this extra information when thinking critically about the explanation and the purpose of the video was probably not specifically to teach students how to use Pi to find the circumference and area of a circle, so adding that would have made the video longer. For the clip itself though, the information would be helpful to include as circumference and area are the point of the clip despite not being the purpose of the video as a whole. 

I love this visualization tool though. I could see this working so well to teach students. Math came quite easy to me as a student, but friends of mine had trouble with these concepts and I believe that this would have greatly expedited their progress.

Every digit after a decimal point is just a smaller and smaller fraction. The philosophers stone.

Author: @crdrost
Content:
This is one of two classic proofs, the other classic proof invites you to create a pizza that is all-nested-crusts and then cut the crusts off of them and unroll them. When you stack them you will get a triangle with base 2πr and height r.

The nice thing about the latter proof is that you don't even need to stack and unstack and unroll everything. Those are the domain of integral calculus, you can do this with differential calculus. What I mean is, think about the crust before the pizza has gone in the oven and topped with toppings. Just plain dough. A scaling argument tells you that A = k r² for some k (when you zoom in on anything by 2x, if it's a line it doubles, if it's an area it quadruples, if it's a volume it octuples...). But what k? Well, wrap a thin ribbon of dough around the pizza, width ε. The ribbon has area 2 π r × ε and the area changes to k (r + ε)² ≈ kr² + 2 k r ε, so it has to be that k = π. (The k ε² is basically that if you do this with a rectangle noodle there is a little "v" when you wrap it around, because the  inradius matches perfectly but the outside radius is off by 2π ε. You _can_ make the argument exact, but most mathematicians would prefer to just shrink the dough ribbon to the width of an atom or so, so that nobody notices the little triangle missing)

Author: @ab_ab_c
Content:
Circle Facts:

    Circumference (C): The length of the outer edge or perimeter of a circle.
    Radius (r): The length from the center of a circle to the outer edge of a circle.
    Diameter (D): The length across a circle from edge to edge through the center.
    Relationship between Diameter and Radius: D=2r.

Circumference and Pi:

    C/D=π≈3.1415926 radians
    C/2r=π≈3.1415926 radians (because D=2r)
    2π=2×≈3.1415926≈6.28318532 radians (is a full circle (circumference) in radians)

From C/2r=π, we can see that C/2=πr.   That means that half of the circumference is equal to πr.

To geometricaally and mathematically prove that the area of the circle is πr², we can think of the area as follows:

    Geometric Interpretation:
        Imagine slicing the circle into many very thin wedges and rearranging those wedges to form a rectangle.
        The length of this rectangle represents half the circumference of the circle, and the width represents the radius of the circle.
        Therefore, the area of this 'rectangle', which approximates the area of the circle, can be thought of as half the circumference of the circle times the radius of the circle (e.g. . A = 1/2 * C * r).  Since we also know that C=2πr, we can substitute it into the previous equation to get: A = 1/2 * 2πr * r = πr² (Note: the twos cancel out to leave us with A = πr²).

The first explanation made perfect sense, the second explanation started relying on select words having intrinsic meaning, and I had to look up five or six of the words he was using cavalierly to explain the area circumference of pi squared r whatever. 

It helps to use the simple languages of simple people to convert complex ideas into digestible explanations. Far too often, smart people start with language that they're comfortable with, ignoring that someone might not speak math. I think they do this because they're proud of themselves, and too lazy to translate their own thoughts more simply. Why is radius a word that means radius? These are the complications of my understanding, getting snagged on other people's throw away words.

Content:
That's cool since, 
Let, circumference = C, Diameter = d
C=3.14*d
C=3.14*2r (d=2radius=2r) 
C=2πr
Also, the circle was separated into many pieces from the center which represents a sector, which is enclosed by two radius and a part of the circumference. Thus, when all of the sectors united to make a single rectangle where: radius part is width, represented in the right and left direction while, in the North and South represents the half of circumference which is πr and area of a rectangle is given by:
Length*breadth= πr*r
Area of circle=πr²

Let’s start with make circle1 with r1 = 1, because we don’t know what the area is then we defined the area of the circle1 A1 = x. Now slice the circle1 to make small slices and make rectangle1. We know that the width of the rectangle1 is equal to r1 = 1, the length of the rectangle1 is equal to half of the circumference circle1 (1/2)*C1, and the area of the rectangle1 is equal to A1 = x. So put all together, width*length = area give 1*(1/2)*C1 = x or C1 = 2*x.
Continue with circle2 with r = 2, assuming that area of circle2 is n times bigger than circle1 give A2 = n*x. Now make rectangle2 and using same approach we get 2*(1/2)*C2 = n*x or C2 = n*x. We can measure and compare C2 and C1 which gives C2 = 2*C1, so n*x = 2*2*x or n = 4.  At the end we get A2 = 4*x and C2 = 4*x.
Continue with circle3 with r = 3, assuming that area of circle3 is n times bigger than circle1 give A3 = n*x. Now make rectangle3 and using same approach we get 3*(1/2)*C3 = n*x or C3 = (2/3)*n*x. We can measure and compare C3 and C1 which gives C3 = 3*C1, so (2/3)*n*x = 3*2*x or n = 9.  At the end we get A3 = 9*x and C3 = 6*x.
Continue with circle4 with r = 4, assuming that area of circle4 is n times bigger than circle1 give A4 = n*x. Now make rectangle4 and using same approach we get 4*(1/2)*C4 = n*x or C4 = (1/2)*n*x. We can measure and compare C4 and C1 which gives C4 = 4*C1, so (1/2)*n*x = 4*2*x or n = 16.  At the end we get A4 = 16*x and C4 = 8*x.
Recap, for r1 = 1 gives A1 = 1*x, for r2 = 2 gives A2 = 4*x, for r3 = 3 gives A3 = 9*x, and for r4 = 4 gives A4 = 16*x, so we can see that A = r*r*x
Recap, for r1 = 1 gives C1 = 2*x, for r2 = 2 gives C2 = 4*x, for r3 = 3 gives C3 = 6*x, and for r4 = 4 gives C4 = 8*x, so we can see that C = 2*r*x
Let put another name for x to pi, then A = pi*r*r and C = 2*pi*r.
Next question is how to define pi?

Author: @HaydenTheEeeeeeeeevilEukaryote
Content:
the area of a whole pizza is πr^2, but the area of a single slice is (1/2)θr^2 (if θ is in radians)

this is because when you think of it, the first formula IS the second. There are 2π radiuses to go around the whole circle, and the change in angle that the radius needs to rotate is 2π radians

so the area of an entire circle using the second formula is 0.5 * 2π * r^2, since θ in this case is 2π, which cancels out into π * r^2

visually this is just grabbing that radius line and rotating it like a clock hand, filling in the area beneath it as it rotates. Once it makes a full revolution of 2π radians, it’s the complete area. But if it only goes at a fraction of that angle, it only gets the radius of that slice
